My main struggle is more about rushing through things, feeling constantly on the go, and impulsively jumping into procedures before I'm supposed to, rather than a lack of attention.\n\nDoctor: Do you have difficulty organizing tasks and activities, or do you avoid tasks that require mental effort, such as preparing for exams or completing paperwork for your radiology program?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really have trouble with organizing my tasks or avoiding paperwork and exams. My main struggles are much more about physical restlessness, rushing through procedures, and blurting things out rather than keeping organized.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience physical restlessness, such as fidgeting or feeling like you're 'on the go,' compared to impulsivity symptoms like interrupting others or blurting out answers?\n\nPatient: Honestly, both happen constantly, but the physical restlessness is like a baseline state where I'm \"on the go\" and pacing from the second I wake up. I'm just so distressed because my dream career is on the line.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any situations where you feel more in control of your restlessness and impulsivity, such as during quiet time alone or when engaged in a highly focused activity, and if so, how do you manage to cope with these symptoms in those situations?\n\nPatient: Even during quiet times or hobbies like sketching or watching a movie, I don't feel in control of my restlessness at all. I constantly catch myself tapping my pen, talking over the show, or making little noises because doing things quietly feels almost impossible. I really don't have a way to cope with or stop these behaviors.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a situation where you were able to control your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, but still experienced significant physical restlessness or hyperactivity?\n\nPatient: During long lectures or safety briefings, I sometimes manage to keep quiet and avoid interrupting, but the physical restlessness is still intense. My whole body feels like it is crawling, forcing me to constantly bounce my leg, shift in my chair, or find excuses to get up. Sitting still like that is almost unbearable for me.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations where you were able to control your physical restlessness, but your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, was still a significant problem?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, I haven't really thought about it that way before. It feels almost impossible for me to just sit there quietly without speaking up or making some kind of noise.\n\nDoctor: Do you also find yourself having difficulty waiting for your turn or interrupting others in lines, conversations, or other daily activities, and do you often feel restless or fidgety when you have to wait?\n\nPatient: Yes, waiting is incredibly hard for me—whether I'm standing in the cafeteria line or waiting to use the CT scanner in lab, I get so tense and fidgety that I feel like I physically can't just stand there. However, I don't really experience other impulsive behaviors like reckless driving or impulsive spending.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you also experience symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus during tasks, making careless mistakes, or struggling to follow through on instructions?\n\nPatient: I don't really have trouble with losing focus or making careless mistakes because my mind is drifting off. My main struggle is more about rushing through things, feeling constantly on the go, and impulsively jumping into procedures before I'm supposed to, rather than a lack of attention.\n\nDoctor: Do you have difficulty organizing tasks and activities, or do you avoid tasks that require mental effort, such as preparing for exams or completing paperwork for your radiology program?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really have trouble with organizing my tasks or avoiding paperwork and exams. It feels almost impossible for me to just sit there quietly without speaking up or making some kind of noise.\n\nDoctor: Do you also find yourself having difficulty waiting for your turn or interrupting others in lines, conversations, or other daily activities, and do you often feel restless or fidgety when you have to wait?\n\nPatient: Yes, waiting is incredibly hard for me—whether I'm standing in the cafeteria line or waiting to use the CT scanner in lab, I get so tense and fidgety that I feel like I physically can't just stand there. During long lectures or safety briefings, my whole body feels like it's crawling, so I'm constantly bouncing my leg, shifting in my seat, or finding excuses to get up because sitting still is unbearable.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel like you're driven to do things without fully thinking them through, such as impulsive spending, reckless driving, or saying things you later regret?\n\nPatient: I definitely say things without thinking them through, constantly blurting out answers and cutting people off before they finish, which I really regret because it gets me into so much trouble. However, I don't really experience other impulsive behaviors like reckless driving or impulsive spending.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you also experience symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus during tasks, making careless mistakes, or struggling to follow through on instructions?\n\nPatient: I don't really have trouble with losing focus or making careless mistakes because my mind is drifting off. My main struggle is more about rushing through things, feeling constantly on the go, and impulsively jumping into procedures before I'm supposed to, rather than a lack of attention.\n\nDoctor: Do you have difficulty organizing tasks and activities, or do you avoid tasks that require mental effort, such as preparing for exams or completing paperwork for your radiology program?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really have trouble with organizing my tasks or avoiding paperwork and exams. My main struggles are much more about physical restlessness, rushing through procedures, and blurting things out rather than keeping organized.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience physical restlessness, such as fidgeting or feeling like you're 'on the go,' compared to impulsivity symptoms like interrupting others or blurting out answers?\n\nPatient: Honestly, both happen constantly, but the physical restlessness is like a baseline state where I'm \"on the go\" and pacing from the second I wake up. The impulsivity, like interrupting and blurting out answers, triggers intensely whenever I'm interacting with people, sitting in class, or trying to wait my turn. It's incredibly frustrating because I feel like I have absolutely no control over either of them.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, is more troubling to you, or is it the constant feeling of restlessness and being 'on the go' that bothers you more?\n\nPatient: While both are incredibly frustrating, the interrupting and blurting things out is definitely much more troubling because it is actively jeopardizing my future. The physical restlessness is exhausting, but cutting people off has gotten me written warnings and put me at risk of being kicked out of my radiology program. I'm just so distressed because my dream career is on the line.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any situations where you feel more in control of your restlessness and impulsivity, such as during quiet time alone or when engaged in a highly focused activity, and if so, how do you manage to cope with these symptoms in those situations?\n\nPatient: Even during quiet times or hobbies like sketching or watching a movie, I don't feel in control of my restlessness at all. I constantly catch myself tapping my pen, talking over the show, or making little noises because doing things quietly feels almost impossible. I really don't have a way to cope with or stop these behaviors.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a situation where you were able to control your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, but still experienced significant physical restlessness or hyperactivity?\n\nPatient: During long lectures or safety briefings, I sometimes manage to keep quiet and avoid interrupting, but the physical restlessness is still intense.
